sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Global Release Times
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is almost upon us, and while Nintendo has yet to make an official announcement about when the Switch 2 exclusive goes live on the eShop, based on previous release times for the company’s big games, we know what to expect. Ocarina of Time is expected to launch at midnight local time globally on November 5, which means that yes, the good old New Zealand trick applies if you really want to get ahead of the game (if you’re in North America, a full day early!). But it’s worth noting that in North America, we’re talking about midnight in the eastern most time zone. So, Zelda goes live at 12am ET on November 5, but 9pm PT on November 4. Make sure you've got enough space on your Switch 2; The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake weighs in at 24.5 GB. As you can see, you can play Ocarina of Time early if you link your Nintendo Account to another region, or create a new account. This process will be familiar to a number of Switch and Switch 2 owners who have already made new accounts just for moments like this. There are other things you’ll need to bear in mind if you're doing the New Zealand trick. You’ll need a New Zealand credit card or eShop cards to add funds to your New Zealand Nintendo Account. And if you do that you’ll end up paying over the odds for Ocarina of Time, relative to how much it would cost in USD. So, you’ll need to really, really want to play a day early to fuss over the New Zealand trick. Nintendo has also announced in-store events at both Nintendo San Francisco and Nintendo New York, if you fancy an old-school midnight launch celebration with fans. As Nintendo has pulled back the curtain on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake , we’ve begun to get a better understanding of how this Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive will look and feel to play. IGN has already got you covered with an extensive hands-on preview , as well as a roundup of all the changes we’ve noticed so far compared to the N64 masterpiece. While you wait for the game to come out, check out a special episode of Nintendo Voice Chat where we dive deeper into our Zelda preview. Meanwhile, we finally have confirmation of who actually developed the Ocarina of Time remake . Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. sources.title: Nintendo Reveals the Changes It Made to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Notoriously Difficult Water Temple for the Remake
sources.text: Nintendo has discussed the changes it has made to the notoriously difficult Water Temple for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. In an interview with Zelda boss Eiji Aonuma, Production Group No.3’s HokWai Ng, and other members of the development team published on the Nintendo website , changes made to dungeons were outlined. Crucially, Aonuma — who worked on the original Ocarina of Time back in the ‘90s — was able to finally get to what he called “overdue homework” on the Water Temple. The original Water Temple in the 1998 N64 masterpiece is infamous for its complex puzzle solving, but also its lack of handholding. This made it a bewildering challenge for many players of the original game. As someone who played Ocarina of Time back in the day — and without the help of a guide — I found the Water Temple pretty frustrating. It took me longer to work out than pretty much any part of the game, as I struggled to make sense of the water levels and locked doors. And don’t get me started on that item toggling. Ng said that Nintendo’s approach with the remake was to retain the dungeon mechanisms from the original game, but improve “playability.” “For example, we placed objects in such a way that players intuitively figure out which direction to go,” he said. “So if you look closely, you may notice areas where the layout differs slightly from the original game.” For Aonuma, the Water Temple was personal. “I wanted to do something about the Water Temple I created 28 years ago,” he said, laughing. “Since it became well known for its difficulty in the original game, I had the team make some adjustments in this version. When I designed the Water Temple all those years ago, I wanted to create an experience where simply being underwater was fun. It was a time when there were very few 3D games that even let players go underwater. I enjoy freediving, and what I find fascinating about being underwater is how different everything feels. The sounds change, and it feels like you’re in a completely different space. I wanted to create a place where players could experience those sensations. “However, with the dungeon’s complex structure and a lot of item toggling involved, you often had to open the menu screen repeatedly, making it hard to keep track of where you were and which way you were facing. We addressed those issues in this version.” To that end, the remake makes item toggling “much easier,” and Nintendo has “changed some of the walls that made it easy to lose your sense of direction to lattice-style structures, making it possible to see the rooms beyond them and get a better sense of the overall space.” Essentially, rather than simply changing the structure to make things easier, Nintendo came up with various ideas to rework it so that players wouldn’t get lost. As IGN’s Logan Plant spotted while viewing Ocarina of Time remake gameplay , the 3DS version’s wall lights, which helped guide players to water-shifting spots, return for the Switch 2 remake. And, as teased by Nintendo today, Link can instantly take off his iron boots without having to pause and go to the equipment menu. There’s a fun exchange at the end of the interview that taps into the immense nostalgia fans have for Ocarina of Time, and what I imagine will be a typical household experience when the remake comes out. “More than anything, I personally would be happy if it became a conversation starter that encourages players of different generations to share memories with each other,” Ng said. “You know, your Dad got stuck in the Water Temple plenty of times back in the day [laughs].” Aonuma: “Then kids playing this version might say, ‘Come on, it’s not that hard.’ Poor old Dad might end up feeling deflated.” While you wait for the game to come out, check out a special episode of Nintendo Voice Chat where we dive deeper into our Zelda preview. Meanwhile, we finally have confirmation of who actually developed the Ocarina of Time remake , and a roundup of the Ocarina of Time remake global release times . Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Link’s Tunic Looks Like That Because He Made It Himself
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time When the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake was first revealed, one of the most common gut reactions I saw across the internet was in response to the game’s overall visual style. And everyone seemed to focus on one thing in particular: Link’s clothes. Basically, Link’s clothes feature a ridiculous amount of detail. They appear to be hand-woven out of some sort of fiber, and you can see every stitch. There’s a fringe around the bottom, and larger stitches where the sleeves attach and where his hat comes together. Over his tunic, he’s wearing some sort of leather armor with swirling leaf designs. Adult Link’s boots have similar etchings. It all looks…not hyperrealistic or anything, but it certainly has an over-the-top amount of intricacy that the Nintendo 64 Link never could have dreamed of. There was debate, though, as to whether this was good or not. Some people compared it to the look of Unreal Engine fan games , which have been oft-mocked for missing the simplistic charm of typical Nintendo games. A lot of people felt that Link stood out from his surroundings, especially when he stood next to other NPCs with less detail, such as some folks in Castle Town. But others really liked the tunic and its details, and noted how well it spoke to Link’s origins as a child of the forest. Well according to the game’s developers, that history is exactly what they were tapping into with the tunic’s intricate look. In an Ask the Developer interview today, art director Aya Shida and producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained how the tunic (and the rest of the art style) came to be. Shida begins by saying the team didn’t take changing the designs lightly, and began by making sketches of the characters to place side-by-side with the old designs, as well as a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree. “We wanted characters like these to blend naturally into a world like this.” The sketches made by the team don’t look more realistic than the old designs. But the original designs did have significant limits placed upon them by the Nintendo 64’s technology, as Fujibayashi explains: Back when games were being developed for Nintendo 64, there were limits to what could be expressed in-game. With those limitations in mind, the developers chose to exaggerate the charactersâ movements and defining features so that their distinctive qualities would come through. But if we recreated all of that precisely with today’s technology, it might look a little creepy. (Laughs) I imagine it was quite a challenge to strike the right balance while still preserving each character’s individuality. Fujibayashi ends by noting that in the new game, there was a lot of attention given to clothing textures now that those limitations have been removed. As an example, Shida offers Young Link’s outfit. If the fabric looked too neat, as though it had been machine-woven, it wouldn’t look like something the children living in the forest had made themselves. It just wouldn’t feel believable. So we started by asking what kind of fabric those children might actually weave and wear. We looked at materials in museums and even experimented with making our own fabric from thread to get a better sense of what it should be like. For this game, the hardware allowed us to depict that level of detail, but that also meant we needed to do our research until we had a clear idea of what we wanted to create. As a design team, we often talked about imagining the story behind every object in the game as we created it. So essentially, while Link’s smooth tunic was fine for the Nintendo 64’s capabilities, on the souped-up Switch 2, a smooth tunic might have looked ridiculous on him and the other Kokiri given what we know about their lore. So instead, the team did a bunch of (frankly very cool) research to work out what sort of clothing would make sense for him and his brethren, clothing which would naturally be quite different from what everyone outside the forest was wearing. The rest of the interview is pretty cool and worth reading, though if you’re just looking for highlights, you can read real quick about Eiji Aonuma adding, and then removing, more fast travel points to the game. A second part to the interview will be out tomorrow, and the remake of Ocarina of Time is out later this week, on November 5. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. sources.title: Nintendo explica por que decidiu refazer Zelda: Ocarina of Time para Switch 2
sources.text: A Nintendo explicou os motivos que levaram à criação do remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time para o Nintendo Switch 2 . Segundo Eiji Aonuma, produtor da franquia, o projeto vai além das comemorações dos 40 anos de The Legend of Zelda , celebrados em 2026. Em entrevista publicada no site oficial da Nintendo, Aonuma revelou que a decisão também está relacionada à evolução da própria equipe de desenvolvimento. Muitos profissionais que atualmente trabalham na franquia participaram apenas dos jogos mais recentes, como Breath of the Wild e Tears of the Kingdom . A proposta é permitir que esses desenvolvedores revisitem a estrutura de Ocarina of Time , lançado originalmente em 1998 para Nintendo 64, e compreendam sua importância para a identidade da série. De acordo com Aonuma, reconstruir Ocarina of Time oferece à equipe uma oportunidade de estudar decisões de design que ajudaram a definir a franquia. O produtor acredita que revisitar o desenvolvimento do clássico pode gerar novas ideias para os futuros jogos de The Legend of Zelda . A intenção não é necessariamente abandonar a liberdade dos títulos mais recentes, mas compreender como elementos tradicionais, como progressão narrativa, exploração e desenvolvimento gradual das habilidades do jogador, podem contribuir para novas experiências. Outro objetivo do remake é aproximar jogadores que conheceram a franquia por meio de Breath of the Wild da estrutura tradicional de Zelda . Enquanto os títulos mais recentes permitem explorar o mundo e escolher diferentes caminhos desde o início, Ocarina of Time apresenta uma aventura com progressão mais direcionada, na qual novos locais, habilidades e acontecimentos são introduzidos gradualmente. Para Aonuma, essa diferença representa uma oportunidade de mostrar outra abordagem de design que também faz parte da história da franquia. O remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time chega em 5 de novembro de 2026 , exclusivamente para Nintendo Switch 2, como parte das comemorações do aniversário de 40 anos da série. sources.title: Nintendo explains why Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake’s auto jump was hard to drop
sources.text: A simple decision to let players jump whenever they wanted has big implications for Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake The decision to drop Link’s auto-jump from Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Nintendo Switch 2 remake was not a simple one, Nintendo has revealed. In a new blog post explaining some of the creative decisions made in the upcoming remake, the game’s developers discuss the issues that arose when trying to modernize Ocarina of Time’s control scheme. The most significant change, they explained, is allowing the player to jump on command, rather than auto-jump kicking in towards a ledge, something which then influenced how the rest of the game was designed. Longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma said that the original game’s auto-jump was a “convenient” design decision, as it meant that the developers had more control over where players could explore. There were restrictions in place, and the environments were designed around this. “If you remove that restriction and make it possible to jump anywhere, you need to anticipate all kinds of player behavior and make corresponding adjustments to the environment,” Aonuma explains. “So at first, we were like, ‘Are we sure about this?’ So, even a single change can instantly increase the number of things that need to be reviewed.” On top of this, Young Link and Adult Link have different jumping distances, so developers had to be mindful that players were always able to pull off leaps regardless of who they were playing as. It is, therefore, no surprise then that the developers have also made changes to the dungeons, since getting rid of the auto-jump opens up many more possibilities. In particular, Aonuma admitted that there have been changes made to the infamous Water Temple, based on years of complaints that it was too difficult. “When I designed the Water Temple all those years ago, I wanted to create an experience where simply being underwater was fun,” Aonuma said. “It was a time when there were very few 3D games that even let players go underwater. “However, with the dungeonâs complex structure and a lot of item toggling involved, you often had to open the menu screen repeatedly, making it hard to keep track of where you were and which way you were facing. We addressed those issues in this version.” More specifically, it’s claimed that players will have better visibility in the new Water Temple, so we won’t get as lost. It should also be easier to toggle between items that we need to traverse the dungeon. That said, Aonuma insisted on keeping some of the original design quirks in the remake. He said that he struggled to adapt to the new Jump Attack, which is now a two-button input. Due to this, players can toggle the controls to make it a single-button input, like in the original release. Aonuma has also stated previously that he is “surprised” that the team did not make more changes in the remake, so it sounds like we are in for a faithful recreation of the original experience.

sources.title: South of Midnight Creative Director Would Have Turned Off Xbox 'Money Tap' Earlier, Says Funding Was 'Unsustainable'
sources.text: David Sears, creative director of South of Midnight, said in a recent interview that he was always worried about the previous era of Xbox's infamous development funding "money tap," and admitted he would probably have turned it off earlier. The Xbox Game Studios-published South of Midnight launched in 2025, seven years after Compulsion Games' previous game came out. While it enjoyed critical acclaim, it failed commercially. Compulsion split from Xbox this year amid CEO Asha Sharma's "reset" of Microsoft's video game business, which has seen thousands of staff lose their jobs, multiple owned studios go independent, and multiple projects canceled. In an interview with MinnMax , Sears said he was always worried Microsoft's generous funding of South of Midnight would end. “I literally told people, I was like, 'Wow, this could be terrible,’” he said. “Because somebody is going to say one day, 'You know the money tap? We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream.” Next, he was asked if he’d have turned off the tap earlier himself if he was in charge of Xbox, to which he replied: “Yeah, probably.” “I wanted to make [South of Midnight], no doubt. Obviously, because we made it,” he continued. “Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. But in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course it was going to have a shocking outcome." Microsoft bought Compulsion in mid-2018 as part of a spate of acquisitions designed to bolster subscription service Game Pass' day-one offering under previous gaming boss Phil Spencer. That summer, Xbox's ranks were swollen by the arrival of Forza Horizon developer Playground, State of Decay developer Undead Labs, Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, the aforementioned Compulsion Games, then, later that year, inXile and Obsidian. Microsoft also formed a new studio in Santa Monica called The Initiative, which worked on the canceled Perfect Dark reboot. Microsoft acquired Double Fine the following year, in June 2019. “It’s easy to dissect it now, but at the time I would talk to other directors who would be like, ‘How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?’ And I would always be like, ‘For now.’ There’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be but I was always worried about it. “But to their credit — amazing. I think there’s definitely a corporate Microsoft DNA, but they are vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the ‘90s and early 2000s — much more humane, actually. It’s remarkable and commendable.” Sears went on to praise Microsoft for letting studios spin off from Xbox rather than shut them down, pointing to how Microsoft bought Ensemble Studios only to shut it down after a couple of games. Like Psychonauts developer Double Fine and State of Decay maker Undead Labs, Compulsion Games secured its independence instead of being closed. Deathloop and Dishonored 2 developer Arkane Lyon, however, is still looking for a buyer as Xbox explores options to split from the studio. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory went through the same process , but didn’t find a buyer and closed as a result. Earlier this year, Microsoft announced that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision , with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios. Xbox has moved Age of Empires developer World's Edge and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under the Activision umbrella. Microsoft is doubling down on its biggest video game franchises as it works to improve revenue at Xbox and grow its profit margin. South of Midnight was Compulsion's third game, following Contrast in 2013 and We Happy Few in 2018. It retains ownership of its games and publishing rights despite leaving Xbox. sources.text: Now free to pursue its own destiny independent of Xbox, South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games has been actively looking for collaborative work with other partners. But given some comments recently made by creative director David Sears, I wouldn’t be surprised if Compulsion’s next project was something very, very different from South of Midnight; after all, Sears doesn’t think that game was a great business decision to begin with. In an interview with MinnMax ‘s Ben Hanson, Sears speaks at length about Xbox’s decision to fund games like South of Midnight and Double Fine’s Keeper , games which he and Xbox knew would probably not make lots of money (and in fact did not) but would increase Xbox’s prestige, or serve as cultural cornerstones for generations to come. However, he also says that he told people during development, “Somebody is going to say, one day, ‘The money tap, we’re closing those floodgates.’ And that’s going to have really traumatic results downstream.” Hanson then summarizes what he thinks Sears is saying. “So the idea is, you’re thankful that Microsoft supported the hell out of South of Midnight …but you would not have funded it yourself?” Sears replied, “Yeah, probably.” He continued: I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight ? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. Of course it was going to have a “shocking” outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, “How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?” And I’d always be like (he sucks in air through his teeth) “For now.” And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it. Sears concludes this thought by remarking that the Microsoft of today is much “more humane” than the company he knew in the ’90s, as demonstrated by the fact that it let studios spin off in the first place instead of just shutting them down entirely. In addition to South of Midnight , Compulsion Games is also known for 2018’s We Happy Few , which it made with Gearbox Publishing. It was acquired by Microsoft just ahead of that release to join Xbox Game Studios, and began working on South of Midnight , which was nominated for and won numerous awards after its launch in 2025, including a BAFTA. Compulsion was spun out from Microsoft as a part of Xbox’s recent restructuring, taking with it all its IP and an unknown amount of financial runway. sources.title: Xbox "money tap" was "unsustainable," says dev who admits he wouldn't have funded his own game
sources.text: The state of affairs at Xbox right now is pretty grim. Microsoft 's games division is letting go of a total of 3,200 jobs after years of declining financial returns. In discussing this, a lead developer for one of the brand's exclusives last year mentions that he probably wouldn't have funded his own game given where things were at. Chatting to MinnMax , David Sears, the co-director of South of Midnight, went into where his reluctance would come from. "I literally told people, I was like, 'Yeah, wow, this could be terrible,'" he says. "Because somebody is going to say one day, the money tap, we're closing those floodgates and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream," he adds. When asked to clarify if he's implying he wouldn't have gotten as behind South of Midnight as Xbox did, he makes it clear that is where he's at. "Yeah. I mean, I wanted to make it, no doubt, right?" he continues. "Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless." That's a big statement to make about your own game, but I can understand his perspective. Xbox has clearly been in a difficult position for a while now, and you could probably highlight a bunch of games that were riskier to fund than perhaps necessary. It sure seems like a lot of people have learned the hard way that the money well wasn't as deep as anyone thought, which has led to the current cutbacks. "It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable," Sears adds. "So, of course, it was going to have a shocking outcome." Hindsight is always 20/20, and at least South of Midnight exists as a result. sources.title: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Name, Logo, Officially Revealed as Bethesda Marks 40th Anniversary
sources.text: Bethesda Game Studios has officially announced the subtitle for The Elder Scrolls 6. The long-awaited follow-up to Skyrim will be called Sentinel, making its official title The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. A logo has also been revealed. Both come as part of a video message from longtime franchise director Todd Howard as Bethesda celebrates its 40th anniversary. The confirmation follows a report from last week that has proven to be quite correct. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma got a demo of The Elder Scrolls VI earlier this summer, and teased the subtitle in her post by replacing the name we now know to be Sentinel with eight asterisks. Turns out those asterisks were very specific then, as Sentinel is of course eight letters. Sentinel is a city within the province of Hammerfell on the continent of Tamriel, where The Elder Scrolls is set. It sits on the northwest coast, nestled beside Iliac Bay. Hammerfell, meanwhile, is located due west of Cyrodiil, where Oblivion took place, and southwest of Skyrim (speaking of which, Bethesda notes that The Elder Scrolls 5 is "still Bethesda Game Studios’ most played game" – and we clarified with Bethesda that this is referring to total lifetime players). Its northern border is shared with the province of High Rock, and its western edge meets the Abacean Sea. It's been a long wait for The Elder Scrolls 6, as it was first announced way back in 2018 , and fans have waited for more information on it ever since. Today's subtitle and logo reveal are the first real bits of news on it in quite some time, though we likely have at least a couple more years to wait before playing it. On Xbox and PC, that is. With Sharma's renewed focus on console exclusives , will The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel even see the light of day on a PlayStation console? That remains to be seen, but it's the biggest card Microsoft has to play in order to get more people back into its ecosystem. For now, though, at least we've got the Sentinel name, and we'll have to cross our fingers that we get a proper reveal at next year's Xbox Showcase in June. sources.text: Bethesda celebrates 40 years with a fresh Elder Scrolls VI teaser. Bethesda celebrates 40 years with a fresh Elder Scrolls VI teaser. Bethesda is officially confirming today that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI Sentinel . The confirmation came in a less than 10-minute video celebrating 40 years of Bethesda game studios. It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series, and studio chief Todd Howard made the announcement today and called it the “perfect time” to fully name the game. Bethesda isn’t sharing any more details on The Elder Scrolls VI Sentinel today, though. The Xbox Wire press release on the name is literally just a picture of the logo. I reported in Notepad last week that Bethesda was planning to name the game in November, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online . Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.

sources.title: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is confirmed, finally getting new trailer and full name, 8 years, 4 months, and 23 days after its reveal
sources.text: Today, Xbox and Bethesda have finally revealed the name and more information about The Elder Scrolls 6. The game, which we now know carries the subtitle Sentinel, was revealed in a special video that took place today, 3rd November 2026, almost exactly 15 years since the launch of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim and eight years, four months, and 23 days since the first reveal of the title card for The Elder Scrolls 6 . That's over 100 months, by the way, or 3067 days, if you want to get specific. In the trailer, a glimpse of the new game - mostly with some fancy sand physics - before the name, Sentinel, is revealed formally. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate," says a quote in the video, attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell. "For 40 years, we've explored new worlds, told unforgettable stories, and gone on incredible adventures together," says a blurb for new video. "From everyone at Bethesda Game Studios , thank you for joining us along this journey, for making these worlds your own, and for inspiring us to keep creating. Here's to 40 more." This reveal comes after a report last week suggested we'd be seeing more of the highly-anticipated fantasy RPG in November, and which also predicted the name of the game. That report suggested that the title will take place in the Tamriel region of Hammerfell, will touch on the "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts". This trailer seems to confirm all that. Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, as a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside . Notably, the reveal of the game is taking place not six months after Bethesda suffered sweeping job cuts (alongside many other Microsoft-owned studios) as part of Xbox's "reset" . So why has it taken eight years for Bethesda to show us this game? Previously, Skyrim's lead designer Bruce Nesmith noted that the studio and boss Todd Howard felt pressured to reveal the game to the world because "the pitchforks and torches were out" . "[...] Todd's opinion - one which I share, by the way - is that the video game industry has short memories," he said in an interview in 2023. "Those companies that start touting their games years ahead of time, actually, you know, they screw themselves. The best time to start talking about it is six months before release." It's worth noting, then, that this is what Bethesda did with Fallout 4 . Does that hint at a timeline for more Sentinel footage being shown soon, and a potentially sooner-than-we-thought release date? Who knows. If we are going to see the game again anytime soon, it's most likely going to be during The Game Awards 2026, which is taking place on 10th December.

sources.text: The long-awaited title of the next Elder Scrolls game was revealed in a video marking Bethesda Softworks' 40th anniversary. Eight years after it was announced , it's finally officially official: The next RPG in Bethesda's long-running Elder Scrolls series is called Sentinel. The title was revealed in a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, narrated by Todd Howard (of course), who cast back to the studio's first game, Gridiron—Bethesda was big on sports games back in the day—before moving into The Elder Scrolls series, the games that would take it to the big leagues, in the early 1990s. "As we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Howard says as the video draws to an end. "And so even though yes, we're looking back,we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called." And thus is the title revealed: Sentinel . There's an interesting quote after the title is revealed: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." Those words were uttered by Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell in the year 4E 206, which was UESP pointed out puts Sentinel at least five years after the events of Skyrim. No other details are revealed, but the title (and that quote) presumably also reveals the setting: Hammerfell, home of the redguards. Sentinel itself is one of Hammerfell's major kingdoms and capital of the Alik'r Desert—reflected in the teaser's sandy backdrop. It's something of a geographical shift from the flyover of the generic mountains seen in that 2018 reveal, although the Alik'r is bordered by the Dragontail Mountains, so who knows. So there you have it! The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. sources.text: Rockstar Games has confirmed the GTA 6 preload and global release times as well as the install size of the game. Code-in-box versions for both consoles “should” be available from retailers beginning November 12, Rockstar added. As for the install size, Rockstar confirmed that the preload file weighs in at up to 212 GB, “depending on your device.” “So make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible,” Rockstar said. sources.text: A Bethesda finalmente revelou uma das informações mais aguardadas pelos fãs de RPG: o nome oficial de The Elder Scrolls 6. O próximo capítulo da franquia será chamado The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel e ganhou seu primeiro logo oficial em um vídeo especial publicado nesta terça-feira (3), durante as comemorações de 40 anos da Bethesda Game Studios. A revelação foi feita por Todd Howard, produtor executivo e uma das principais figuras da desenvolvedora. No vídeo comemorativo, o executivo relembra a trajetória do estúdio e comenta a relação dos jogadores com seus games antes de anunciar que a ocasião seria perfeita para revelar como o novo The Elder Scrolls realmente se chama. Apesar da novidade, a Bethesda não apresentou imagens de gameplay, detalhes da história ou uma previsão de lançamento. Em uma publicação separada, a empresa também alertou que “ainda vai demorar algum tempo” até estar pronta para compartilhar mais informações sobre o projeto. O nome Sentinel já era alvo de rumores e especulações há algum tempo. A escolha também reforça teorias da comunidade de que o próximo RPG da Bethesda será ambientado em Hammerfell, uma das províncias do continente de Tamriel. Sentinel é uma cidade localizada no noroeste de Hammerfell, próxima à Baía de Iliac, região que separa as províncias de Hammerfell e High Rock. O território já apareceu em outros jogos da franquia, incluindo The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, The Elder Scrolls Online e The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard. A região também é mencionada em uma citação trazida no fim do teaser apresentado pela Bethesda. O texto em questão diz o seguinte, na tradução para o português brasileiro: “O pergaminho revelou apenas um vislumbre, um véu sutilmente erguido diante dos meus olhos. Um futuro perdido. Uma vitória desfeita. Areias do tempo espalhadas pelo destino.” — Yazar, Sacerdote das Mariposas da Alta Rainha Iradne de Hammerfell (4ª Era, ano 206). A possibilidade de explorar essa região também alimenta teorias sobre a presença de mecânicas inéditas na série. No mês passado, Bruce Nesmith, ex-desenvolvedor da Bethesda e designer principal de Skyrim, comentou que gostaria de ver os rumores sobre a ambientação se confirmarem. Segundo ele, o cenário poderia abrir espaço para a utilização de barcos e exploração marítima, algo que ainda não teve grande destaque na franquia. A confirmação do subtítulo chega após uma espera considerável dos fãs. The Elder Scrolls VI foi anunciado originalmente em 2018, durante a E3, mas a Bethesda praticamente não compartilhou novidades concretas sobre o projeto desde então. Na semana passada, uma reportagem do The Verge indicou que a desenvolvedora poderia revelar o nome do jogo ainda em novembro. A expectativa era de que o anúncio acontecesse próximo ao aniversário de 15 anos de The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, lançado originalmente em 11 de novembro de 2011. Outro detalhe curioso surgiu em uma publicação recente de Asha Sharma, CEO do Xbox. Ao comentar uma demonstração de The Elder Scrolls VI que teria recebido durante o verão no hemisfério norte, a executiva utilizou oito asteriscos para esconder o subtítulo do jogo — exatamente a quantidade de letras de Sentinel. Por enquanto, a Bethesda mantém o mistério sobre os próximos passos do RPG. Considerando o longo período desde o anúncio original e a falta de informações sobre o desenvolvimento, ainda não há previsão oficial de lançamento ou confirmação de plataformas além do ecossistema Xbox e PC. A possibilidade de uma versão para PlayStation também segue sem resposta. Enquanto isso, a empresa destacou que Skyrim continua sendo o jogo mais jogado da história da Bethesda Game Studios, considerando o total de jogadores ao longo de sua trajetória. O novo capítulo terá a difícil missão de suceder um dos RPGs mais populares de todos os tempos, além de atender as expectativas dos fãs que esperam pelo novo jogo há anos. sources.text: From grappling mutants to cyborg tanks, discover which kaiju is right for you. With its giant-sized fanbase, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has plenty of players ready to get tooth, nail, and claw stuck into its PlayStation 5 release on November 3. Although it would be understandable that newcomers might feel a little intimidated choosing between 12 world crushing kaiju, each with their own stats, moveset, and special abilities. Never fear – we have the rundown on which colossus matches your playstyle to ensure you’re the true king of the monsters. Ideal for: Players who want to dive straight in. The face which sank a thousand ships. Godzilla is the iconic kaiju who all other kaiju want to be, beat, or be friends with. As the game’s default character, the giant lizard is balanced for newbies and veterans alike, with a high amount of starting health and decent all-round stats. Godzilla also possesses a tail useful enough for a mighty wake-up strike when he’s downed, and some fairly swift claws, so many of his melee combos are effective for beginners. But don’t rely too much on his high-energy pulse – while it’s formidable, the slow charge leaves him open to counters. Similarly, ranged attackers can take advantage of his relatively sluggish projectiles, so close that distance or you’ll be heading back to Monster Island with your giant tail between your legs. Ideal for: Players annoyed at their friend for picking Heisei Godzilla. In terms of film history, Godzilla 2000 is a more modern incarnation of the legendary lizard, reflecting a new era for the new millennium. Although he’s arguably a slightly more vulnerable version of his Heisei predecessor. As a result, while Godzilla 2000 is a bit faster than his kaiju shoto fighter twin, he’s not quite as strong. He’s still fairly well balanced and arguably easier to use than Heisei, so makes for a solid alternative. And his distinctive purple dorsal plates look pretty cool, too. Ideal for: Players who want to control the battlefield. There’s a reason why this fearsome three-headed beast is seen as Godzilla’s archnemesis. Giant wings, gravity beams, and a desire to annihilate humanity, the threat of King Ghidorah should never be taken lightly. Given his monstrous size it shouldn’t be a surprise that the ‘supreme ruler of the cosmos’ isn’t the fastest kaiju on the block, but he’s resilient and a perfect ‘zoning’ character, capable of keeping foes at a distance with a variety of projectiles. His flight is a little limited due to its energy drain, but it’s balanced by a lightning blast that has no charge while airborne. However, despite his colossal wings, Ghidorah’s lack of arms and stubby legs makes him a poor melee fighter. Ideal for: Players who think defense is the best offense. He might look a bit like Godzooky with more spikes, but mutant dinosaur Anguirus is one of Godzilla’s most loyal allies – even if his track record against other kaiju hasn’t been the best in the movies. The Monster Island citizen is fast and aggressive, but his low power and lack of long-range attacks means Anguirus is best utilized as a counter-attack specialist. His block might be on the slow side due to its turning animation, but it actually damages an attacking opponent due to Anguirus’ rear spines. With his high defense and solid grappling skills, this mutant shouldn’t be underestimated. Ideal for: Players who love to hit and run. Given its status as a guardian to the ancient underground civilisation of Seatopia, Megalon is more of an antagonist than an out-and-out villain in Godzilla lore. While not quite as domineering as its colossal rivals, the subterranean kaiju is still capable of putting a hurt on with its drill-like appendages. Megalon’s primary advantage is its tunnelling skill which not only allows it to avoid attacks, but also pop-up and grab opponents. Even though burrowing uses energy, it still makes Megalon a difficult fighter to pin down, especially when used in tandem with its myriad of electricity attacks. On the flip side, Megalon isn’t the most durable of beasts with below average defense. Stick and move, or die. Ideal for: Players wanting to attack with deadly speed. One of the most sadistic fighters to hail from M Space Hunter Nebula, cyborg kaiju Gigan is easily one of Godzilla’s more vicious adversaries. Despite being defeated multiple times, the hook-clawed Gigan just keeps coming back for more. Unsurprisingly, Gigan’s tenacious approach makes him perfect for aggressive rushdown tactics. He’s not only swift, but his teleportation ability gives him incredible range and evasion skills. And those hooks aren’t for decoration either, delivering damage-heavy edged strikes. His Laser Eye is a little unwieldy, and he’s vulnerable to energy attacks, but Gigan remains a versatile option for anyone wanting a decent melee and range mix-up. Ideal for: Players wanting a classic tank character. Known as ‘death incarnate’, everything about Destoroyah is built to intimidate. Giant wings, clawed hands, taloned feet… this mutant crustacean almost has it all. Which is to say, Destoroyah is one of the more powerful creatures in the game with brutal physical assaults and a wide variety of high-damage – and often unblockable – energy attacks that truly make him the perfect mid-range monster. But there’s a cost. Destoroyah’s best abilities are extremely power hungry, so without them he’s potentially ineffective given how painfully slow his movement is. Ideal for: Players wanting speed above all else. With his dominance of the skies and fearsome pteranodon looks, you’d be fooled into thinking Rodan is an out-and-out villain, but he’s more a force of chaos, even capable of being selfless in some parts of Godzilla lore. True to type, Rodan is not only the fastest monster in the game, but also the most mobile in the air. sources.text: Lançamentos de games em NOVEMBRO de 2026 - Calendário VOXL Além do aguardado GTA 6, novembro traz remake de Ocarina of Time e mais de 30 jogos. Confira as estreias do mês. Crédito: Voxl Sempre fui um grande fã de kaijus e de toda essa cultura de criaturas e robôs gigantes. Por isso, quando soube que Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee receberia uma versão remasterizada, fiquei bastante empolgado. Sempre tive vontade de jogar esse clássico, lançado originalmente em 2002 para Nintendo GameCube e Xbox, mas nunca tive acesso às plataformas necessárias na época. Agora, mais de duas décadas depois, finalmente tenho a oportunidade de conhecer esse jogo em uma versão voltada para os consoles e computadores atuais. Com a chegada de Godzilla Minus Zero , sequência de Godzilla Minus One prevista para novembro de 2026, o momento também parece propício para resgatar um clássico da porradaria entre monstros gigantes. Afinal, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee tem aquela energia dos jogos que você reúne os primos para jogar, sem compromisso com o realismo ou com uma narrativa complexa, apenas para trocar golpes, destruir cenários e dar boas risadas. É um tipo de diversão descompromissada que não se leva tão a sério — e isso faz parte do seu charme. Desenvolvido originalmente pela Pipeworks Studios, o jogo coloca kaijus conhecidos da franquia em confrontos nos quais prédios e outros elementos do cenário também fazem parte da pancadaria. A versão remasterizada busca preservar essa experiência, atualizando a apresentação visual e levando o combate para plataformas modernas, além de incluir recursos como partidas online. Mas, quando um jogo clássico retorna depois de tantos anos, surge uma questão importante: por que modernizar apenas os gráficos e os recursos técnicos? Relançamentos também são oportunidades para rever aspectos da experiência que vão além da resolução das imagens ou do desempenho. Controles mais flexíveis, opções gráficas ajustáveis e recursos de acessibilidade podem fazer a diferença para que mais pessoas consigam aproveitar um jogo. Isso é especialmente relevante em títulos de ação, nos quais acompanhar vários personagens na tela, identificar ataques em meio a explosões, interpretar informações da interface e executar comandos no momento certo pode representar uma barreira para jogadores com deficiência. É com essa perspectiva que analiso Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered . Além de revisitar um clássico que sempre tive vontade de experimentar, quero entender quais recursos de acessibilidade estão disponíveis nessa nova versão, quais barreiras permanecem e até que ponto o relançamento aproveita a oportunidade de adaptar essa experiência às necessidades de jogadores com deficiência. Afinal, destruir cidades com monstros gigantes pode ser uma diversão para muita gente, mas essa diversão só será realmente acessível quando mais jogadores puderem participar dela. Vale ressaltar que a acessibilidade é uma experiência individual e se aplica de maneira diferente a cada pessoa, de acordo com suas necessidades e características. Portanto, as impressões apresentadas nesta análise partem da minha experiência pessoal como pessoa com baixa visão. Meu objetivo é destacar os recursos de acessibilidade presentes no jogo, explicar como eles podem contribuir para uma experiência mais inclusiva e apontar as barreiras que encontrei durante os testes. Essas observações não pretendem representar a experiência de todas as pessoas com deficiência, mas contribuir para que mais jogadores conheçam as possibilidades e limitações oferecidas pelo título. Aviso de transparência: Esta análise foi realizada com uma chave de acesso antecipado disponibilizada pela equipe de Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered para PS5, antes do lançamento oficial do jogo. O título é desenvolvido pela Pipeworks Studios e publicado pela Atari. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered oferece legendas, mas não permite alterar o tamanho ou personalizar sua apresentação. Também não há opções de legendas ocultas ( closed captions ) que identifiquem sons importantes do ambiente e dos combates, o que pode dificultar o acompanhamento das partidas por jogadores surdos ou com deficiência auditiva. Um dos pontos mais decepcionantes é a falta de opções para personalizar os controles. Mesmo sendo um relançamento para plataformas modernas, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered não oferece remapeamento de comandos nem ajustes mais detalhados para adaptar a jogabilidade às necessidades de cada pessoa. Essa limitação pesa especialmente em um jogo de luta e ação no qual é necessário executar diferentes comandos durante confrontos movimentados. Sem a possibilidade de reorganizar os botões, jogadores com deficiência motora podem encontrar dificuldades para realizar determinadas ações ou simplesmente não conseguir configurar os comandos de uma maneira confortável. A ausência de alternativas também reduz a flexibilidade para quem precisa de uma configuração específica por questões de mobilidade ou coordenação. É frustrante que uma versão remasterizada não aproveite a oportunidade para incluir recursos tão importantes. Atualizar os gráficos e levar o jogo a plataformas atuais não é suficiente para modernizar a experiência quando os controles continuam sem opções básicas de personalização. A vibração do controle pode ser ativada ou desativada, mas esse ajuste pontual está longe de compensar a falta de remapeamento. Nas configurações de áudio, o jogo permite ajustar separadamente o volume da música, dos efeitos sonoros e das vozes dos personagens. Essa divisão oferece algum controle sobre a mixagem, mas não é acompanhada de recursos específicos que ajudem jogadores com deficiência auditiva a identificar os acontecimentos durante as partidas. sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts
sources.text: Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs. In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN ). "Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department." This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted" . Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well". Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run. Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time , "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone. While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle . "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained. "We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead." Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein , so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

sources.title: Doom studio is "doing great" despite Xbox cutting half its staff, studio head insists
sources.text: We're still not sure what's next for either team A total of 3,200 jobs will be cut at Xbox by the end of this fiscal year as part of an extensive restructuring. One of the casualties already is id Software , which has lost somewhere in the region of half its staff. That said, if you ask current leadership, everything at the Doom and Quake studio is fine and dandy at the moment. Marty Stratton, studio co-director of id Software, commented on how the company's been doing since the layoffs hit over the summer during a preview event for Doom: The Dark Ages DLC. "We're doing great," he says, per IGN . "Not to handwave the [layoffs] away," he adds. "Everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that. But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department." Being down half your team is pretty significant. Reportedly, id Tech itself, the studio's in-house engine, is now being managed by exactly one whole person . While that's certainly viable financially, I'm not sure how structurally sound that is long-term. Stratton goes on. "We're working more closely with MachineGames than ever," he states. "We've always had a very close partnership with them, but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]." A question mark has loomed over MachineGames since the release of Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The prevailing rumor is Wolfenstein 3, and given the general push toward established IP Xbox has been making amid all the redundancies, that seems a safe bet. But what the collaboration between the two companies looks like, and where that leaves the next Doom, are bigger questions. "We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that," Stratton adds. "We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead." sources.title: 'Go Play GTA 6, We Need to Detox,' Wardogs Developer Tells Fans as It Prepares to Take December Off
sources.text: After the runaway success of Wardogs , a new sandbox multiplayer shooter in Early Access on PC, the team at Bulkhead is taking a well-deserved break — and they want you to know you can take a break, too. It’s a break the team likely needs. Since launch, there’s been balance patch after balance patch, hotfixes, major updates, and small updates. Wardogs even saw some controversy when it attempted to region lock players to prevent cheating. Speaking to Edge Magazine, via GamesRadar , Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer explained the pressure the team had been dealing with. "Everyone has done something that's not in their job description,” Brammer said. “Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product." Following a flurry of updates and a disappointing Wardogs Season 2 launch , Bulkhead is taking the whole month of December off to rest and refresh for the new year and the road to the game’s 1.0 launch. "We're going to make sure players know they can f**k off in December," he said. "Go play GTA 6 , we need to detox.” It’s a refreshing approach to hear a developer acknowledge the incoming leviathan that is Rockstar’s open-world crime sequel. Most publishers are just quietly changing their plans with no outward communication, but Bulkhead addressed the massive, massive elephant filling the room. GTA 6 is out on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox, and it is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. A number of publishers and developers either worked to release their games beforehand, leading to the September crunch, or push them back into early 2027. Star Citizen chief Chris Roberts claimed he delayed spinoff Squadron 42 into next year because he didn't want it going up against the "attention buzz saw of GTA 6." "While GTA 6 isn’t launching on PC this November, pretty much all outlets and most content creators will be all over it, not leaving a lot of room for other coverage," Roberts continued. Analysts expect GTA 6 will make over $5 billion in launch week alone , so expect it to fill your feeds for a few weeks. Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

sources.text: The Wardogs team is planning to take a long break to celebrate the success of its early access release, and CEO Joe Brammer knows that it'll probably be fine because players will have plenty to occupy them – in the form of GTA 6 . Speaking to Edge Magazine, Brammer explains that the team has worked hard to earn the right to play hard. "Everyone has done something that's not in their job description. Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product." With the early access launch of Wardogs in the rear-view, the entirety of developer Bulkhead Studios will be taking an extended break, with leave stretching throughout the entire month of December. It's a bold strategy, but one that Brammer is quick to double-down on. "We're going to make sure players know they can fuck off in December," he says, suggesting the team does have some idea of the backlog of bug reports and balance complaints that could be waiting for them come January. The hope, clearly, is that those players will be too distracted by something else to be blasting the Bulkhead forums: "Go play GTA 6, we need to detox," Brammer says. With most games wondering how they'll hope to hold onto their audiences once Rockstar drops its nuke – and Fortnite offering near-unlimited freebies to certain lucky players – it's almost refreshing to see a team unapologetically accepting that its fans will have something else on their minds, and hoping that they'll come back once they're finished with Leonida.
